rows.description: I count who got the bigger piece and cry "not fair!" Fairness matters hugely to me. A wise family lets one child cut and the other choose. I learn that equal is not always the same as fair, but that takes years.

A friend says "I will not share with you, you are not my friend". It stings. I can say "that makes me sad" and go play elsewhere. I should not be blamed for wanting a share, and a teacher can help us take turns.

I see a classmate's shiny box and want it so much my tummy hurts. Envy is normal at this age. Wise action: name the feeling, ask for a turn, or say "I wish I had that". The harmful pattern is hiding it or telling lies about it.

My parent says "give it to him right now" before I am ready. I feel angry and confused because it is my favourite thing. Better help is "you may keep it special, but pick another to share". Forced sharing can make a child hold tighter.
My parent says I am beautiful just as I am, though I do not believe it. Even so, it plants a seed. Being loved unconditionally helps me build a steady view of myself.
Films and ads show only fair, slim, perfect people. I begin to feel I am not good enough. I remember that images are edited and that real people come in every shape and shade.
A classmate teases me about my weight, height or skin colour. It cuts deeply. Their words reflect their unkindness, not my worth; I can tell a trusted adult and seek kind friends.
I feel strong and happy after winning a race. Feeling proud of my body for what it can do is healthy, and I can respect other bodies that are different from mine.
I find a hundred-rupee note in the corridor, and my heart races with ideas of what I could buy. Wanting is natural; a wise choice is handing it to a teacher or asking whose it is.
The shopkeeper gives me extra change by mistake. Nobody will know, but I would. Returning it feels awkward for a moment and then makes me feel light and trusted.
My parent hears that I returned a wallet and hugs me. I feel proud, but I should do the right thing even when nobody praises me, because honesty is for me first.
Friends say, finders keepers, let's buy chips. I feel torn between fitting in and doing right. I can decline politely, and often a friend quietly feels relieved that someone said it.
After a big fight, neither of us wants to speak first. Pride is the barrier. The wiser one offers a small gesture like sharing a snack. Saying sorry does not mean I lose; it means I value us.

My younger brother used my sketchbook without asking, and I shout. My anger is fair, since my things are mine. Wise: tell him calmly, ask a parent to set a rule, and lock away precious things. Hitting or breaking his toy solves nothing.
My little sister follows me everywhere and touches my stuff. It irritates me, but she looks up to me. A wise older sibling sets kind limits: this is mine, but we can play together at five.

I feel my parents love my sibling more because they give them more attention. Often it is different needs, not less love. I ask for one-to-one time and say what I feel, rather than trying to become the trouble child.

When I am ill I cling to Mummy and do not want her to leave. I feel afraid and helpless. Wise: she stays close when she can and tells me when she will be back. Clinging is a request for safety, not naughtiness.
My sibling is sick and gets all the attention and treats. I feel jealous and even wish I was sick too. This is normal. A wise parent gives me some care time and explains the sick child needs rest.
I am scared of the doctor's needle and cry. My heart thumps. A wise adult tells me the truth: "it will pinch for a second and I am here". Lying that it will not hurt makes the next visit harder.
I have a fever and Mummy holds me and sits by my bed. I feel small, warm and safe. Being cared for while sick teaches that I can be weak and still loved, and that resting is okay.

Your smaller firm fears a bigger competitor's tactics. Focus on niches and customer relationships where you are better, and protect key clients and staff. Fear can push improvement, but must not push unethical shortcuts.
You lose a bid and feel envy at the rival's win. Ask what they did better: price, trust, service. Study and improve. Public sneering or bad-mouthing them harms your own credibility.
